text: Tiruppur, in Tamil Nadu, is India's knitwear capital. Last year it exported forty six thousand crore rupees of garments, and sells thousands of crores more inside India, almost all through small businesses.
Yet the trade still runs on trade fairs. Buyers travel to Tiruppur to see the goods. Those who can't, buy through local wholesalers and resell, paying extra at every step.
Meanwhile, makers sit on unsold and over produced stock. In one festival season, seventy percent of garments sold came from old stock.
And every day, a seller sends the same photos to ten different buyers on WhatsApp, and chases each one on the phone, often in a language they don't share.
What if we could bridge that gap? That's why we built Claire Connect. One chat app for the whole trade, built on Nexconn.
Buyers ask Claire, our AI assistant, to find the right makers. Both sides deal in their own language, from sample to order. And makers track every step of production.
Here's Amit, a buyer in Kolkata. He asks Claire for a thousand cotton T-shirts. Claire finds makers in Tiruppur, ranked by price, trust and delivery.
He opens a chat with Lakshmi Garments. Two phones, live on one Nexconn channel. Amit writes in English, Lakshmi reads it in Tamil, and her reply reaches him in English.

First, a sample, to check the fabric and the stitching. The quality is good, so he offers ninety rupees for a thousand pieces. Claire gives him a private tip that only he can see. Lakshmi counters at ninety four, he accepts, and the order, with GST, appears on both phones.

Winning the order is only the start. Murali, the maker, cuts and packs in his own unit, but everything else happens outside. He buys fabric, sends it to a dyer, cuts it, sends pieces for printing and stitching, packs, and delivers. Every one of those hand offs can be tracked.
He sends cut pieces to a stitching unit in a few taps. The record lands in their shared chat. Priya confirms what she actually got, and if two pieces are short, both of them see it.
And at any moment, he can see where all five hundred pieces are. At which unit, in his shop, on the way, or with a buyer.
He can even ask his own Claire, in Tamil, and the answer comes only from his own records.
If something goes wrong, like a late payment or a short delivery, the Trade Desk sends a human agent. She joins the same chat, reads what happened before she joined, and sorts it out.
All of this runs on Nexconn. Channels, message cards, translation and calls.
Tiruppur aims to reach one lakh crore rupees in exports by twenty thirty, and almost every business in it is small. Claire Connect gives each of them a direct line to buyers, and to each other.
Claire Connect. Every business in the chain, in its own language, in one chat.
